data.title: Nvidia's early salary increase aims to boost employee morale.
data.description:
Interim CEO Colette Kress reassured employees at an all-hands meeting as former founder Jensen Huang sought to regain control of the company. Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, promised to give employees a raise and new stock awards in December, ahead of schedule. The chip giant's new leadership is trying to boost employee morale following Jensen Huang's resignation. At an internal all-hands meeting on Wednesday, Kress appeared alongside other company executives, demonstrating unity. This came a day after Nvidia's new chairman explicitly ruled out Huang's return. According to sources, Kress told employees at the meeting that Nvidia would be issuing the raise and new round of stock awards in December, breaking with the company's usual practice of conducting annual employee reviews in the spring. Following Jensen Huang's resignation, Nvidia's stock price fell, raising concerns among employees that their stock-based compensation would be reduced. Since announcing Huang's departure, Nvidia's stock price has fallen 13%, wiping out approximately $500 billion in market value. Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, speaks at Wednesday's all-hands meeting. Wednesday's meeting and the salary increase decision provided Kress with an opportunity to boost morale. According to two attendees, the meeting concluded with Tom Petty's "I Won't Back Down," and employees waved their phone flashlights in the air. The night before this meeting, Kress hosted Nvidia's quarterly earnings call for the first time as CEO. She announced strong financial results and raised the company's sales forecast. Earlier that day, Jensen Huang made his first public statement since resigning on Tuesday afternoon. The Nvidia founder stated that he was willing to return to lead the company. He also said that after his resignation, "Nvidia employees, investors, business partners, and customers have been urging me to return as CEO." Over the past weekend, a growing online campaign calling for Huang's return, driven by tech executives like Elon Musk and investors, has gained momentum. Nvidia employees have also signed online petitions and voiced their opinions on social media. Huang is highly respected by many Nvidia employees. Compared to other large tech companies, Nvidia has an unusually low employee turnover rate. Jensen Huang's departure caused a rift between some employees and the board. However, newly appointed chairman Harvey Jones stated on Tuesday that Huang resigned voluntarily after disclosing "behavior that was inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms." Jones explicitly ruled out the possibility of Huang returning to the company. Jones stated that the company will consider both internal and external candidates to finalize the selection process for a new CEO as soon as possible. Meanwhile, the board is conducting an independent investigation led by a former federal prosecutor. Sources familiar with the matter said Jones also attended Wednesday's internal meeting. Several long-time Nvidia executives were also present, including Huang's co-founder Chris Malachowsky and Ian Buck, head of the data center business.

Kress, who has served as Nvidia's CFO for over a decade, acknowledged during Tuesday's analyst call that there are differing opinions within the company regarding CEO succession. She said, "Like any group, there are different voices here."

Kress stated, "But we believe our employees remain fully committed. They are dedicated to achieving their life's work at Nvidia… During this transition period, we will take care of our employees, ensure their safety, and ensure that all work can proceed smoothly in the current environment."

data.title: The largest IPO in history will ring the bell tonight: Can Anthropic reach $100?
data.description:
The IPO is unlikely to break its issue price on the first day, but it's unlikely to replicate SpaceX's 30% intraday gain.

Anthropic (Nasdaq: ANT), the first AI stock of the 21st century, will officially debut on Nasdaq tonight.

On November 18, Anthropic completed its IPO fundraising and pricing, issuing a total of 980 million Class A ordinary shares, raising $81.3 billion. Including the previous $26 billion private placement, Anthropic's total fundraising amounted to $107.3 billion, surpassing SpaceX to become the largest IPO in human history.

Anthropic's Class A ordinary shares were priced at $83 per share, higher than the previously given guidance range of $70 to $78 per share.

Anthropic's Class A ordinary shares were priced at $83 per share, higher than the previously given guidance range of $70 to $78 per share.

Based on approximately 18 billion fully diluted shares, Anthropic's fully diluted valuation is about $1.5 trillion, ranking 15th globally in market capitalization, second only to Tesla. However, market expectations for Anthropic's closing market capitalization on its first day of trading are not optimistic. Polymarket data shows that the market bets 58% that Anthropic's closing market capitalization will be between $1.25 trillion and $1.5 trillion, only 16% that it will exceed $1.5 trillion, and a mere 1% that it will reach $2 trillion. This probability distribution contrasts sharply with the enthusiasm shown by investors during the Anthropic IPO subscription. Anthropic originally planned to issue 825 million shares, but due to overwhelmingly higher-than-expected demand from both institutional and retail investors (Odaily note: institutional investor demand was approximately $400 billion, and retail demand was close to $100 billion), the company ultimately increased the issuance size to 980 million shares and raised the offering price from the upper limit of the guidance range of $78 to $83. So, is it that the market believes there is no potential upside after expanding the IPO size, or has the supply and demand relationship for Anthropic stock reached complete equilibrium? In this case, how will Anthropic perform on its first day of trading tonight? Should investors who have already participated in the IPO subscription take profits tonight? Are there still opportunities for investors who did not participate in the subscription to enter the market? Odaily Planet Daily will provide a brief analysis in this article for investors' reference only. **Highest First-Day Circulation: 7.19%, Structurally Biased** While this IPO set a record for issuance size, the actual percentage of shares entering the public market is very low, exhibiting a typical high FDV (Funded-to-Volume) and low free float structure. Based on a fully diluted share capital of approximately 18 billion shares, Anthropic's IPO issuance of 980 million shares represents only about 5.44% of the total share capital. Of these, 956.35 million shares were issued by Anthropic itself, and the remaining 23.65 million shares were sold by the co-founders. Adding to this the 315 million shares previously disclosed in Anthropic's prospectus that could be sold from the first trading day, theoretically, a maximum of 1.295 billion shares would be available for trading on the first day, representing approximately 7.19% of the total 18 billion shares. Low liquidity incentivized underwriters to support the price on the first day of trading. Anthropic's underwriters also had a very useful tool – the greenshoe option. Anthropic granted underwriters the right to purchase up to 147 million additional shares, valid for 30 days. Based on the offering price of $83, this represents approximately $12.2 billion in funding. The greenshoe option was originally designed to address price volatility in the early stages of an IPO. If the share price falls below $83 after listing, underwriters can buy shares on the secondary market to cover short positions created by over-allotment. This not only absorbs some market selling pressure but also provides room for maneuver regarding whether to exercise the greenshoe option later. Conversely, if Anthropic performs strongly on its first day, underwriters can exercise the greenshoe option to purchase additional shares at the offering price, fulfilling their over-allotment obligation. Of course, this doesn't mean there's absolute price protection at $83, but given the limited free float on the first day and IPO demand far exceeding the offering size, the underwriters' price stabilization mechanism undoubtedly provided additional support for Anthropic's stock price. Therefore, considering only the free float and the underwriting mechanism, the probability of Anthropic's stock price falling significantly below the offering price on its first day of trading is relatively limited, and its short-term trend is likely to be more upward. Anthropic's first-day performance may mirror SpaceX's. In June of this year, SpaceX priced its IPO at $135 per share and officially listed on Nasdaq. The stock price immediately jumped to $150, an increase of approximately 11% over the offering price. During the day, the price fluctuated wildly, reaching as high as $176, a 30.4% increase, but ultimately closed at $160.95, a 19.2% increase over the offering price. Anthropic shares similarities with SpaceX: both are trillion-dollar companies with high fully diluted valuations and low free float, both accumulated significant unsubscribed demand before their IPOs, and both had high retail investor participation. The difference lies in their businesses: SpaceX's core is launches and satellite networks, while Anthropic's core is a large-scale model. In terms of retail investor participation, Anthropic may break SpaceX's record. According to Vanda Research, Anthropic is expected to attract approximately $250 million in net retail buying on its first day of trading, more than double the $118 million net retail buying seen on SpaceX's opening day. This is a positive for Anthropic because retail investors are typically less constrained by strict valuation models than institutional investors, making them more likely to create a buying frenzy in the early stages of a hot IPO. Investors who didn't secure sufficient allocations during the IPO subscription are likely to buy in the secondary market. However, retail investors influence volatility, not the final price increase. SpaceX's intraday high and closing price fluctuated by 8% on its first day of trading. Retail investors can buy indiscriminately due to FOMO (Fear of Missing Out), and they can also sell impulsively at the slightest fluctuation. Anthropic's IPO comes at a time when sentiment in the AI ​​sector has cooled significantly, a major external difference from SpaceX's IPO. Previously, Nvidia's management changes had already dragged down the sector for several days, and even Nvidia's better-than-expected earnings report failed to reverse the downward trend. Furthermore, investor concerns about slowing capital expenditures and delayed returns in the AI ​​industry continue to intensify. Many institutions are using Anthropic's first-day performance as a key indicator of market enthusiasm for AI companies. Overall, Anthropic is likely to close above its IPO price on its first day, but replicating SpaceX's 30% intraday gain is unrealistic. How much premium will it open with? Currently, market disagreement regarding Anthropic's first-day performance is concentrated around $100. Based on the offering price of $83, the aforementioned target price still has a potential upside of approximately 20%, corresponding to a market capitalization of $1.8 trillion. According to Hyperliquid data, Anthropic's pre-market contracts are also fluctuating between $99.95 and $100. Many underwriters, such as Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, are unable to provide valuation and target price opinions for Anthropic due to the quiet period, but some independent institutions have provided their views before the pricing was finalized. Morningstar analysts previously believed that the Anthropic IPO price range of $70 to $78 per share reflected a decline in market sentiment towards AI rather than Anthropic's fundamentals. They believed Anthropic's fair value was priced at $92 per share, equivalent to a market capitalization of $1.7 trillion, representing a 10% upside potential based on the latest offering price. Morningstar analysts also provided a long-term outlook for Anthropic, predicting a 47% revenue growth rate over the next five years, which would push its stock price to $188. However, if corporate adoption slows and Anthropic loses its competitive advantage, the stock price could fall to $25. Kennedy, senior market strategist at Renaissance Capital, believes Anthropic's closing price on its first day of trading could reach $100. New Street set a 12-month price target of $105 for Anthropic stock, believing its annual revenue could surge to over $500 billion. Freedom also set a target price of $101.90 per share, bullish on Anthropic's enterprise customer growth. Of course, some investors believe Anthropic is not worth its $1.8 trillion valuation and have taken short positions. According to on-chain data, a whale held approximately $90 million in short positions related to Anthropic on Hyperliquid through two wallets, with orders placed between $98 and $102, and currently has a floating profit of over $1.58 million. [Image of the whale's two wallets] Regardless of whether the bulls or bears win tonight, the Anthropic IPO is destined to be a watershed moment for the AI ​​industry.

data.title: Anthropic IPO Creates Wealth: These Billionaires Are the Biggest Winners
data.description:
On the evening of November 18th local time, AI giant Anthropic announced its IPO on the 19th, with a fully diluted valuation of $1.5 trillion. The net worth of the company's seven co-founders and three billionaire investors subsequently increased significantly. [Image source: (from left to right) GETTY IMAGES/Visual China/Visual China] On the evening of the 18th, the highly anticipated Anthropic initial public offering (IPO) price was finalized at $83 per share. On a fully diluted basis, the AI ​​giant that created the Claude chatbot is valued at $1.5 trillion. CEO Dario Amodi and the other six co-founders' combined net worth increased by $40 billion, totaling approximately $140 billion, or about $19.9 billion per person. The combined net worth of three early investors in Anthropic also increased by $9 billion. They are former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Dubai luxury real estate developer Hussein Sajwani, and Estonian Skype co-founder and AI security advocate Jan Tallinn. Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven former employees of competitor OpenAI. Forbes previously estimated the value of these billionaires' stakes based on the company's last private funding round in May of this year—when the stock price, adjusted for a stock split, was $58.90 per share, corresponding to a valuation of $965 billion. Reportedly, before the tech stock crash of the past month, some Anthropic investors had expected an IPO valuation of $2 trillion. Last week, the company disclosed an IPO price range of $70 to $78 per share, corresponding to a fully diluted market capitalization of between $1.3 trillion and $1.4 trillion. Anthropic's IPO will raise at least $79.4 billion, with a concurrent private placement raising an additional $26 billion from tech giants such as Google, Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron Technology, Microsoft, TSMC, and AMD. In terms of total fundraising, Anthropic's offering will be the largest IPO in history, surpassing SpaceX's previous record of $86.3 billion raised without a private placement, resulting in a fully diluted valuation of nearly $1.8 trillion. Anthropic shares will begin trading on Nasdaq on March 19th under the ticker symbol ANT. The seven co-founders, after selling a total of $2 billion worth of stock in the IPO, collectively hold nearly 9% of the company's equity, with each holding roughly equal shares. However, they collectively hold one non-economic equity share with 50.1% of the voting rights, thus retaining control of the newly listed company. The co-founders have pledged to ultimately donate 80% of their personal holdings to philanthropy. However, Anthropic's prospectus states that this commitment is revocable and not legally binding. Schmidt, with a current net worth of approximately $46.6 billion, participated in Anthropic's $124 million Series A funding round in 2021 and currently holds approximately 0.9% of the company's equity, valued at $13.6 billion. Tallinn, with a net worth of $17 billion, led the Series A funding round, at which time Anthropic's valuation was reportedly less than $500 million. He now holds approximately 1% of the equity, valued at $15.6 billion. Sajwani, with a net worth of $16.7 billion, holds 0.1% of Anthropic's equity, valued at $1.9 billion, nearly three-quarters of which was purchased in 2024 for $50 million from Sam Bankman-Fried's bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX. FTX's investment has more than doubled its initial $500 million stake, but if it hadn't been forced to sell all its Anthropic shares for $1.3 billion two and a half years ago, it would now hold a 2.5% stake in the AI ​​giant, worth $37 billion. The following are the biggest billionaire winners created by Anthropic's IPO. (Net worth data as of November 18 closing. Anthropic's equity value is calculated based on the IPO price of $83 per share.) Dario Amodei Estimated shareholding: 1.3% Estimated market value of shares: $19.6 billion (previously $14.1 billion) Estimated net worth: $19.8 billion (previously $14.1 billion) Image source: Visual China The 43-year-old Amodei holds a PhD in biophysics from Princeton University and has worked for Chinese tech giants Baidu and Google Brain. He first worked as Brain, and later rose to the position of Vice President of Research at OpenAI, the company that developed ChatGPT. In late 2020, due to disagreements with the company regarding security principles and commercialization paths, he and several colleagues who would later co-found Anthropic left the company. In addition to his personal shares in Anthropic, Amodi also holds voting rights in company stocks held by charitable entities such as "donor-advised funds," representing a market value of $384 million. In an article published in January of this year, he argued that artificial intelligence could widen the wealth gap, and that the ultra-wealthy have a responsibility to address this issue. Daniela Amodei

Estimated shareholding: 1.3%

Estimated market value of shareholding: $19.7 billion (previously $14.1 billion)

Estimated net worth: $19.8 billion (previously $14.1 billion)

Image source: Visual China

The 39-year-old Daniela is currently the president and chairman of Anthropic, overseeing the company's business operations. Her brother, Dalio, serves as CEO, leading research and development. Daniela graduated from the University of California, Santa Cruz with a degree in English Literature. She previously worked in politics and global health before joining the payment giant Stripe as an early employee. She joined OpenAI in 2018, rising through the ranks to become VP of Security and Policy, before leaving in 2021 to co-found Anthropic. In the two tender offers in June 2025 and April 2026, the Amody siblings were the only two co-founders to disclose their share sales, though the specific size of the sale is unknown. Daniela's husband, Holden Karnofsky, co-founded the charity Coefficient Giving in 2011 with Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz and others; the organization is associated with the effective altruism movement. Karnofsky joined Anthropic in 2025 as a technologist. Christopher Olah

Estimated stake: 1.3%

Estimated market value of stake: $19.8 billion (previously $14.2 billion)

Estimated net worth: $20 billion (previously $14.2 billion)

The 34-year-old Olah is the youngest co-founder of Anthropic and the only one of the seven without a college degree and the only non-US citizen. Born in Canada, he dropped out of the University of Toronto and was selected for the Thiel Fellowship in 2012, subsequently joining Google Brain and later leading the explainability team at OpenAI. He now leads Anthropic's explainability research, aiming to reverse engineer the internal workings of AI models to uncover potential vulnerabilities that could lead to errors or security risks.

... Eric SchmidtEstimated stake: 0.9%Estimated market value of stake: $13.6 billion (previously $9.7 billion)Estimated net worth: $46.6 billion (previously $42.7 billion)>

Image source: TAYLOR HILL/FILMMAGIC/GETTY IMAGES

The 71-year-old Schmidt, a former Google CEO, participated in Anthropic's $124 million Series A funding round in 2021, when the startup was reportedly valued at less than $500 million.

His acquaintance with Dario Ammoddi was facilitated by his ex-girlfriend, Cami Clark, who later became Ammoddi's wife. Schmidt led Google from 2001 to 2011 and will become CEO of rocket startup Relativity Space from 2025. Over the years, he has sold more than $5 billion worth of stock in his former employers, but still holds shares in Google's parent company, Alphabet, worth approximately $23 billion. Hussein Sajwani

Estimated shareholding percentage: 0.1%

Estimated market value of shareholding: $1.9 billion (previously $1.4 billion)

Estimated net worth: $16.7 billion (previously $16.1 billion)

Image source: JACOPO RAULE/GETTY IMAGES

The 73-year-old Sajwani is the founder and chairman of DAMAC Group, a high-end real estate developer in Dubai. He indirectly holds shares in Anthropic.

In 2024, he bought nearly three-quarters of his current stake from FTX's bankruptcy liquidation assets for $50 million. The remaining quarter is held through a fund of Lightspeed Venture Partners, which participated in Anthropic's Series E funding round in 2025, when the company was valued at $61.5 billion. "In less than two years of investing in Anthropic, I earned what I had accumulated in 30 years of business," Sajwani said last week at a Bloomberg event in Dubai. He is a longtime business partner of Donald Trump, owns a Trump-named golf course, and also holds stakes in several AI companies, including OpenAI, xAI (now part of SpaceX), and Mistral.

Jaan Tallinn

Estimated shareholding: 1%

Estimated market value of shareholding: $15.6 billion (previously $11.1 billion)

Estimated net worth: $17 billion (previously $12.5 billion)

The 54-year-old Tallinn is an Estonian programmer who co-founded Skype in 2003. After eBay acquired Skype for $2.6 billion in 2005, he used the proceeds to become one of the earliest investors in the field of artificial intelligence, investing in the AI ​​lab DeepMind three years before Google acquired it in 2014. In 2021, he led Anthropic's Series A funding round, and participated in a $580 million Series B round the following year. According to PitchBook, the Series B funding round valued Anthropic at $3 billion.

Tallinn has long been concerned that advanced artificial intelligence may pose an existential threat to humanity, and co-founded the Cambridge Centre for Survival Risks and the non-profit Future of Life Institute. Jack Clark, 38, born in the UK, previously covered artificial intelligence at Bloomberg before joining OpenAI as Director of Policy in 2016. He now heads public interest affairs at Anthropic and is expected to be one of the first managers of the company's subsidiary, the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. This fund focuses on public issues and philanthropic projects and holds nearly 5% of the newly listed company's shares, valued at $66.1 billion. Clark has also been writing an AI industry newsletter called *Import AI* since 2016. Jared Kaplan Estimated stake: 1.3% Estimated market value of stake: $19.8 billion (previously $14.2 billion) Estimated net worth: $19.9 billion (previously $14.2 billion) The 42-year-old Kaplan is currently the Chief Scientific Officer of Anthropic. Before entering the AI ​​field, he was a theoretical physicist at Johns Hopkins University. In 2020, while consulting for OpenAI, he co-authored a paper with Sam McCandless, who later co-founded Anthropic, on scaling laws, demonstrating that the performance of AI models systematically improves with increasing training data volume and computing power. This discovery has become the underlying business logic for the entire industry's massive investment in data centers. Kaplan graduated from Stanford University with a double degree in physics and mathematics, and later obtained a PhD in physics from Harvard University. Tom Brown, 39, is Anthropic's Chief Computing Officer. In 2020, he published the OpenAI GPT-3 research paper as the first author; this model is the technological foundation for the later ChatGPT. Before joining OpenAI, he worked at Google Brain and co-founded two startups after graduating from MIT. At Anthropic, he is responsible for managing the company's massive computing power business. According to the company's prospectus, Anthropic has signed computing power procurement contracts totaling approximately $900 billion by 2045. Sam McCandlish's estimated shareholding: 1.3% Estimated market value of shareholding: $19.8 billion (previously $14.3 billion) Estimated net worth: $20 billion (previously $14.3 billion) Image source: ANTHROPIC The 36-year-old McCandlish is the most low-profile of Anthropic's seven co-founders. He was the company's first Chief Technology Officer and later became Chief Architect. He is a theoretical physicist by training, holding a PhD from Stanford University. He led research at OpenAI, where he co-authored the foundational scaling law paper with Kaplan, who later co-founded Anthropic.
